Aerial Wildlife Survey Report 
Wildlife Management Unit 511 Aerial Ungulate Survey (2025) 
Background 
Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 511 is located in 
north-central Alberta, covering an area of 5798 km2. 
Bounded by the Town of Slave Lake to the west and 
Wabasca to the north, WMU511 is bordered by 
highways 764 north, highway 813 east, the Athabasca 
River in the southwest and in the southeast the 
township baseline between TWP 71 and 72 and the 
boundary of Calling Lake towards highway 813 (Fig. 1). 
The last population estimate of moose in this WMU was 
completed in 2014 where a population decline of 64% 
(90%CI -49—79) had been reported between the most 
recent surveys in 2003 and 2014, with an estimated 
annual population growth rate of 0.91 (90%CI 0.87-0.94) 
during the interval between surveys.  
F
igure 1. Wildlife Management Unit WMU511 in north 
central Alberta. 
S
lave Lake and Nipisi woodland caribou 
population recovery  
This WMU includes portions of two local population units 
of boreal woodland caribou, the Slave Lake and Nipisi 
populations (Fig. 2). The majority of occupancy of the 
Slave Lake population has been constrained to the 
WMU511 portion of the Slave Lake range, east of the 
town of Slave Lake. While the majority of the area for 
Nipisi local population unit occurs in WMU542 to the 
north of 511, the subunit dominated by the Lower 
Foothills Subregion, known as Marten Hills, that is used 
by the Nipisi population unit is within WMU511.  Annual 
wolf reductions were initiated in 2023 in response to 
declines in these caribou populations and have 
continued. While the declines in these caribou 
populations have slowed following wolf control, avoiding 
extirpation, the wolf control measures also reduce 
predation in deer and moose populations. This reduction 
in predation pressure on moose and deer can result in 
the growth of alternative prey populations to densities 
that can be counterproductive to caribou recovery 
objectives (i.e. apparent competition). Therefore, to 
address overabundant populations that could reduce the 
efficacy of predator reductions it is critical to monitor the 
response of moose and deer populations to inform 
potential management actions where predator control 
has reduced natural moose mortality. 
T
he objective of this survey (2025) was to update the 
estimated population size, density and ratios for sex and 
age classes of moose, and to record observations of 
other ungulates during the survey. An additional 
objective was to evaluate the response in ungulate 
populations to the caribou recovery management 
actions, and therefore, this survey was completed in a 
stratified design with WMU350, an adjacent WMU to the 
southwest of WMU511, to provide an estimate of moose 
population parameters for areas within and surrounding 
the Slave Lake local population, and the portion of Nipisi 
range that extends into WMU511.

Survey Method 
The aerial survey for moose in WMU 511 was 
conducted between January 30 and February 6th, 2025. 
Transects, up to 10 km in length and oriented north-
south (Fig. 3), were established throughout the unit with 
1.2 km spacing between transects.  
Figure 3. Survey areas with randomly selected 
transects that were completed during the survey 
(orange) across Wildlife Management Units 350 and 511. 
Sampling design 
Transects were surveyed by selecting a random sample 
of these transects, iteratively by random seed each day. 
Each WMU was stratified into 2 broad landscape strata 
(low and high) based on an index of spring vegetation 
productivity and evaluating encounter rates for moose 
from historic datasets. The Enhanced Vegetation Index 
was used as a proxy for spring green-up approaching the 
calving period for moose. An aggregate dataset of 
annual mean EVI indices of the 16-day period ending on 
June 1, with 500m resolution, was used to generate a 
relative index for the study area (Fig 4). The Enhanced 
Vegetation Index are derived from normalized 
reflectance of red, near-infrared and blue spectrum from 
the MODIS system (NASA AppEARS) and provide a 
relative comparison of greenness of vegetation in the 
canopy (Didan et al., 2015). The initial sampling effort 
follows the random assignment of transects across the 
WMU, regardless of strata, but the efficacy of the 
additional strata are used to iteratively evaluate the 
efficacy of changing the sampling intensity based on 
these strata if the sampling coverage across all strata 
were adequate (sufficient representation and coverage 
across all areas of the WMU), the precision would be 
improved, and survey costs would be decreased due to 
improved gains in precision.

S
urvey method 
T
he distance sampling transect method (Buckland et al. 
2001, Alberta Environment and Parks 2016) used to 
estimate population density and abundance in the study 
area. Surveys are conducted with three observers in Bell 
206 Helicopters with installed bubble windows. The rear 
observers are responsible for the detection of animals 
from the skid to the horizon, and the front left observer 
detects animals directly below the aircraft between the 
skids (e.g., the chin bubble of the BH206 configuration). 
Transects are surveyed with an approximate altitude 
between 100-150m above treeline, and at an airspeed 
between 90-110 km/h. When an animal is observed a 
waypoint on the transect and over the animal group are 
collected to calculate the perpendicular distance that is 
used to model the pattern of detection used to correct for 
the bias in the declining detection with distance from the 
aircraft. In addition to strata within WMU511, the 
concurrent survey of WMU350, immediately adjacent, 
with equivalent survey design and methods were used in 
the analysis to increase robustness of detection models.  
Ungulates were classified by age (adult or young) and 
sex (determined primarily by presence of a vulva patch). 
The category of moose activity (bedded, standing, 
moving) and canopy cover, or vegetation cover within 10 
m of the moose (0-33%, 43-66%, and >66%), were 
included as covariates to improve estimates of detection 
probability and detection bias associated with the survey. 
Although late winter surveys occur after antler drop has 
occurred for many individuals, the size of antlers were 
recorded for all species, when present (Alberta 
Sustainable Resource Development 2010). 
W
hile distance sampling estimates already account for 
the components of precision error (i.e. detection 
probability except at g(0), encounter rate sampling 
variance, and group size variance), applying a bias 
correction (i.e. sightability bias correction), or estimating 
cohort-specific abundance (i.e. cows, bulls, calves) 
requires an additional procedure to address the variation 
in bias correction models and composition ratio error 
estimates. Therefore, to address this additional 
uncertainty we used an integrated Monte Carlo modelling 
procedure to incorporate variance in the bias correction 
model and composition ratio estimates into abundance 
estimates across cohorts.

Results 
A total of 1327km across 255 transects wer e sampled 
for a total of 27.5 hours of flight time, including 
deadhead. This effort corresponds to a survey coverage 
of 20.6% of the total area within the WMU (1194km2 of 
survey coverage). Survey conditions wer e c onsidered 
excellent for most of the survey, although snow and 
extreme cold temperatures prohibited flights on s ome 
days during the survey period. The iterative evaluation 
of the encounter rates and precision did not warrant 
differential sampling effort in the strata, however, 
estimates with and without the additional strata were 
included in the analysis.  
In total, 202 moose were observed on transects from 
131 independent group observations. A total of 180 
moose were classified of which 78 were cows, 51 were 
calves and 51 were bulls. Of the bulls observed, 47% 
had already shed their antlers at the time of the sur vey. 
Of those that still had antlers (n=27), 21 were 
considered small (small spike or forked antlers) and 5 
were medium (palmated, spread less than half the 
length of body). Fifty-nine percent of cows wer e 
observed with a calf at-side, and of those 5 cows had 
twins (10.9% twinning rate). No lone calves were 
observed during the survey. 
The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios wer e 0.654 (90% C I 
0.46-0.85) and 0.666 (90% CI 0.55 – 0.80), respectively. 
The prevalence of hair loss/rub typically associated with 
winter tick was low with only 3 individuals (1.6%) with 
slight tick rub (<25% of total body surface). The density 
estimate was
 0.257 moose/km2 with a coefficient of 
variation (CV) of 10.8% (90% CI 0.21-0.30). The 
uncorrected estimated moose population for WMU 511 
was 1488 (90% CI 1222 -1747). See Table 1 for a 
comparison to previous survey results using the relative 
uncorrected estimates. The mean density and 
abundance estimate corrected for detection bias 
(‘sightability’) at g(0), was 1735 (90%CI 1509-2000) 
moose with an estimated detection probability of 86.3% 
(90CI 74.2-98.3%) across the entire survey. The moose 
population is estimated to have increased by 14.7% 
since the 2013/2014 survey, representing an annual 
average (geometric mean) population growth rate of 1.06 
(90% CI 1.03 - 1.11). 
Most white-tailed deer had shed their antlers, and only 2 
adults were observed with antlers at the time of the 
survey (1 small and 1 medium). Therefore, adult deer 
could not be reliably assigned to sex classes and 
composition ratios were not calculated. In total, 278 
white-tailed deer were observed on transects from 125 
independent group observations. A total of 88 white-
tailed deer were classified of which 55 were antlerless 
adults, 31 were fawns and only 2 were classified as 
bucks.  
The fawn:antlerless adult ratio was 0.583 (90% CI 
0.38-0.79). The density estimate was 0.51 white-tailed 
deer/km2 with a coefficient of variation (CV) of 10.7% 
(90% CI 0.42-0.60). The uncorrected estimated white-
tailed deer population for WMU 511 was 2982 (90% CI 
2460 - 3504). This is the first survey with sufficient 
observations to support an estimated population density 
for this WMU, and therefore comparisons to previous 
estimates are not possible. This is the first survey with 
sufficient observations to support an estimated 
population density for this WMU, and therefore 
comparisons to previous estimates are not possible 
(Table 3).
